ux_screens.screen_name: Neo4j Browser Query Editor & Result View
ux_screens.description: Main editor interface with query execution panel on left, results displayed in multiple modes (graph visualization, tabular output, text/code). Connection bar at top with database selector.
Left sidebar with Query execution tab, central graph canvas for visualization, results panel. Supports custom styling, monitoring, and collaboration features.
Drag-and-drop visual query construction interface. Schema design on left, canvas for pattern drawing, query preview/execution. Supports no-code graph analytics for non-technical users.
Console-based query interface with syntax highlighting. Results displayed in graph visualization panel below. Data import and schema management panels available.
Zero-ETL graph query interface. Query editor supporting both SQL and graph query languages (Cypher, Gremlin). Visualization via PixiJS or integrated gdotv. Supports real-time multi-hop queries.

ux_flows.flow_name: Neo4j: Execute Query and Explore Results
ux_flows.goal: Run a Cypher query and explore results in graph visualization

steps.action: Click in query editor pane
steps.friction: None

steps.action: Type or paste Cypher query
steps.friction: Requires Cypher knowledge

steps.action: Click Run button or press Ctrl+Enter
steps.friction: Button is accessible

steps.action: Results appear in default mode (graph), may need to click result mode tabs to switch views
steps.friction: Multiple tabs to explore; graph mode may be cluttered (hairball antipattern)

steps.action: Click on nodes or use filters to explore relationships
steps.friction: Requires understanding of filtering, zooming, and layout algorithms

ux_flows.our_approach: MetroGraph reduces this to 3-4 clicks: unified query-to-viz in single surface, automatic layout optimization, semantic filtering integrated into initial query construction, no mode-switching friction.

ux_flows.flow_name: Memgraph Lab: Query, Style, and Share Results
ux_flows.goal: Execute query, customize visualization styling, and share with team

steps.action: Open Memgraph Lab on localhost:3000
steps.friction: Low; web-based access

steps.action: Click 'Query execution' tab in left sidebar
steps.friction: Sidebar navigation clear

steps.action: Type or paste Cypher query, click 'Run query' button
steps.friction: Requires Cypher syntax knowledge

steps.action: Results display in graph canvas; click on Graph Style Script (GSS) panel to customize styling
steps.friction: GSS syntax learning curve for non-experts

steps.action: Click sharing button to share query or styling with team
steps.friction: Sharing feature requires enterprise version

steps.action: Team member accesses shared query via link or history
steps.friction: Collaboration features strong; improves team workflow

ux_flows.our_approach: MetroGraph embeds sharing and styling in the main query construction, eliminating separate GSS panel. Collaborative styles are version-controlled alongside queries. No enterprise paywall for core sharing.

ux_flows.goal: Build and execute a graph query using drag-and-drop visual pattern matching

steps.action: Open GraphStudio and navigate to Visual Query Builder tab
steps.friction: Tab navigation clear

steps.action: Drag vertex types from schema panel onto canvas to define pattern nodes
steps.friction: Drag-and-drop is intuitive; reduces Cypher knowledge barrier

steps.action: Draw edges between vertices to define relationships; configure filters and limits
steps.friction: Edge creation is visual but filter panel may feel cramped

steps.action: Click 'Execute' button; results display in visualization below
steps.friction: Low; immediate visual feedback

ux_flows.our_approach: MetroGraph extends this with unified data/relationship palette (not separate schema panel), inline filter suggestions based on query semantics, and instant query-plan visualization showing estimated rows per hop—enabling non-experts to optimize without trial-and-error.

ux_flows.goal: Query relational data as a unified graph without prior ETL; support both SQL and Gremlin/Cypher

steps.action: Connect data source (PostgreSQL, Iceberg, Redshift) via connection string or UI form
steps.friction: Low if connection credentials pre-configured

steps.action: Click 'Auto-map relational schema to graph' or manually define entity/edge mapping
steps.friction: Auto-mapping is powerful; manual mapping adds complexity

steps.action: Type SQL or Gremlin/Cypher query in unified editor; query language selector visible
steps.friction: Query language switching is explicit but clear

steps.action: Execute query; results visualized in PixiJS canvas or exported; performance metrics displayed
steps.friction: Real-time query execution with sub-second latency is major advantage; visualization is lightweight

ux_flows.our_approach: MetroGraph formalizes the SQL↔graph translation as a first-class UI construct: SQL query builder paired with visual pattern matcher, bidirectional mapping inspector, and explicit 'query cost' indicators showing which parts of the pattern are expensive in the relational substrate—eliminating hidden N+1 surprises.

ux_flows.flow_name: NebulaGraph: Data Import and Interactive Console Query
ux_flows.goal: Import data files, define schema, and execute nGQL queries interactively

steps.action: Open NebulaGraph Studio; click Import Data tab
steps.friction: Low; sidebar navigation

steps.action: Upload CSV/JSON file or select remote data source; map columns to vertex/edge types
steps.friction: High friction: schema mapping is modal and text-heavy; no drag-and-drop column mapper

steps.action: Review mapping, configure import parameters, click Import
steps.friction: Import queue may be opaque; no progress feedback

steps.action: Navigate to Console tab; type nGQL query
steps.friction: nGQL syntax not as widely known as Cypher

steps.action: Execute query; results appear in table below; click Visualization tab to see graph
steps.friction: Results split across two separate views; mode-switching required

ux_flows.our_approach: MetroGraph combines import + query in a single unified environment: live schema preview as you map (not a separate modal), incremental import feedback with row counts, and query results with inline visualization toggle (not separate tab)—reducing mode switches and hiding latency with progressive rendering.

ux_patterns.description: User must click tabs or toggle buttons to switch between query editor, graph visualization, table view, and text output. Each mode hides the others, forcing context loss.
ux_patterns.our_rationale: Mode-switching creates cognitive load and breaks flow. MetroGraph surfaces query editor + graph canvas + result metadata simultaneously in a single pane, with inline toggles only for density control—not primary navigation.

ux_patterns.description: All five products require learning a specialized query language (Cypher, nGQL, SQL, Gremlin) to interact with graphs. Non-technical users hit a wall immediately.
ux_patterns.our_rationale: MetroGraph's visual query builder (inspired by TigerGraph's approach) is the default path, with Cypher/SQL as an optional advanced mode. Semantic suggestions auto-complete patterns based on schema + prior queries, reducing barrier from 'memorize syntax' to 'recognize shapes.'

ux_patterns.description: When showing heavily connected graphs, the visualization becomes an unreadable tangle of nodes and edges. Users see cognitive overload, not insight. Compounds with large result sets from unbounded queries.
ux_patterns.our_rationale: MetroGraph detects high-degree nodes and dense regions at query-time, auto-grouping them into collapsed 'super-nodes' with expandable detail. Enables overview-zoom-filter-detail (Shneiderman principle) without post-hoc cleanup. Paired with result limit suggestions in the query panel.

ux_patterns.description: Visualization styling is controlled via external Graph Style Script (Memgraph/Neo4j) or JSON configs (NebulaGraph), requiring a second language and separate panel. Styling is decoupled from query definition.
ux_patterns.our_rationale: MetroGraph unifies query + styling in a single domain language. Inline style hints (e.g., 'high-risk nodes = red') are suggested alongside filters and aggregations. Styles are part of the query artifact, versioned together, not separated into a parallel stylesheet.

ux_patterns.pattern: Flight-to-Chat (LLM Query Generation without Visual Validation)
ux_patterns.description: When query builders or consoles offer LLM-assisted query generation (Memgraph's GraphChat, etc.), users may skip visual pattern validation and execute LLM-generated queries without understanding them, leading to wrong results or performance disasters.
ux_patterns.our_rationale: MetroGraph uses LLM as a pattern *suggester*, not a query generator. LLM outputs are shown as visual patterns (drag-drop nodes + edges) that users can validate, edit, and refine *before* execution. Query plan + estimated cost displayed before run. Eliminates blind trust; keeps human in the loop.

ux_patterns.pattern: Modal Schema Mapping (Data Import in Separate Dialog)
ux_patterns.description: Data import (NebulaGraph, TigerGraph) is hidden in a modal or separate tab. Users lose sight of the main query builder. Mapping columns to entities requires text entry or clumsy dropdown chains.
ux_patterns.our_rationale: MetroGraph shows data sources and schema inline with the query builder. Import flows are progressive: preview → sample rows → confirm mapping → go—all in one surface. Column-to-entity mapping is drag-drop, with visual feedback showing how many rows will become nodes.

ux_patterns.pattern: Performance Blindness (No Query Cost Visibility Before Execution)
ux_patterns.description: Users can execute complex multi-hop queries (e.g., 5+ hops, millions of intermediate results) without any indication of cost, latency, or row explosion. Leads to long-running queries, timeouts, frustration.
ux_patterns.our_rationale: MetroGraph shows estimated query cost alongside the visual pattern: rows per hop, memory footprint, predicted execution time. Users can interactively adjust limits (LIMIT, filter predicates) and see cost update in real time. For external data sources (PuppyGraph use case), shows which parts of the pattern are relational vs. computed.

ux_patterns.pattern: Large Multi-Pane Layouts (3+ Panes, Narrow Columns)
ux_patterns.description: Neo4j Browser, Memgraph Lab, TigerGraph use 3-pane layouts: query editor (left), graph canvas (center), result panel (right). Works for desktop but creates friction on laptops and tablets. Panes compete for width.
ux_patterns.our_rationale: 3-pane layout is justified on large screens (24"+) but breaks on 13–15" laptops. MetroGraph uses responsive stacking: on small screens, collapses to 2-pane (query + viz) with right-sidebar toggles for result metadata. On large screens, expands to 3-pane. Pane widths adjust based on content density (e.g., large result sets widen result panel automatically).

ux_patterns.pattern: Unbounded Query Results (No Default Limit, Large Clutter)
ux_patterns.description: Queries often return thousands or millions of rows, visualized with all nodes shown, creating hairball effect and browser lag. No sensible default limit (e.g., LIMIT 100 for exploration mode).
ux_patterns.our_rationale: MetroGraph defaults to LIMIT 50 for exploration, with a prominent warning if query is unrestricted. Results are streamed progressively; user sees first 50 instantly, can load more in batches. Aggregation + sampling options shown inline ('show 100 most central nodes' vs. 'show all').

notes: Phase C extraction focuses on 5 target products (Neo4j Browser, Memgraph Lab, TigerGraph GraphStudio, NebulaGraph Studio, PuppyGraph). Quantified metrics (pane_count, click_depth, total_clicks, hci_cost) are derived from official documentation, GitHub repositories, and UX research (Cambridge Intelligence, PuppyGraph blog, academic papers on graph visualization). No proprietary Gartner reports or closed usability studies were available; all findings are from publicly documented interfaces. MetroGraph's 'lower-friction approach' reflects best practices from Ben Shneiderman (overview-zoom-filter-detail), Tamara Munzner (visualization task taxonomy), and modern design patterns (visual query builders from Timbuctoo, Graphistry). Flight-to-chat antipattern reflects emerging concern about LLM-assisted queries without validation (cited in GraphChat, Memgraph docs). All source_ids are traceable to sources.json.
